payload.data: 18 April 1942. Sixteen Army B-25s and eighty men ride aboard Hornet. Their plan: strike Japan, then fly on to Chinese airfields. The screen clock is Japan time; ship reports run one hour ahead.

The Japanese picket No. 23 Nittō Maru has seen the force. Nashville opens fire; the warning cannot be recalled. Halsey must protect his carriers. The bombers will leave much farther from Japan than planned.
The order reaches Hornet at 07:00 Japan time. Lashings come off and crews start their engines. Added fuel tanks and weight reductions give the bombers a chance of reaching China.
Doolittle is away. His own report puts take-off at 08:20 ship time; Hornet records 08:25.
The aircraft leave one by one. Each carries five men. They cannot return to land on Hornet; the carrier force will retire east while the bombers continue west.
Farrow’s crew launches last. All sixteen are airborne. The naval reports place the final take-off one or two minutes later.
Hours over the Pacific. Low flying reduces the chance of detection, but navigation and fuel are unforgiving. These paths join reported anchors; they are not recorded flight tracks.
Doolittle reaches the coast north of his intended approach. He turns toward Tokyo from the north. Training aircraft and fighters are visible, but the raid retains much of its surprise.
At about 12:30 Japan time, Doolittle drops incendiaries over Tokyo’s industrial districts. The aircraft then returns to low altitude and heads toward the sea.
Holstrom meets fighters with an inoperative turret. He jettisons his bombs offshore and turns away. The replay places this episode approximately; his attack minute is not established.
Other crews strike factories, oil and power facilities across Tokyo. Bombs also fall among homes. These are reported target districts; smoke seen by crews cannot establish the full damage.
Greening attacks a site he identifies as a refinery east of Tokyo. Bower bombs the Yokohama area. Their intended targets and the places they report hitting are not always the same.
McElroy attacks Yokosuka naval yard at about 13:40 Japan time. His crew reports a crane and a ship in the building slips hit. The replay does not turn that report into a confirmed sinking.
The western aircraft continue toward Nagoya and Kobe. Osaka appeared in planning, but the checked accounts put Hilger and Farrow at Nagoya and Smith at Kobe.
Hilger reports four incendiary attacks at 14:20 Japan time: barracks, oil storage, an arsenal and aircraft works. Farrow also attacks Nagoya; his detailed contemporary report is unavailable.

Smith attacks Kobe’s waterfront and aircraft industry. The raid kills civilians as well as damaging industrial sites. Its overall military damage is limited; its psychological effect will be much larger.
Fifteen bombers are making for China. A helpful tailwind extends their reach. Doolittle’s navigator records passing near Yakushima; the other routes are approximate corridors.
York turns toward the Soviet Union because of fuel consumption. He lands near Vladivostok. The USSR is neutral toward Japan: his five-man crew is interned, not immediately sent home.
Rain, cloud and darkness hide the Chinese coast. Secrecy and the early launch have also disrupted preparations at Chuchow—modern Quzhou. The crews cannot make the planned refuelling landing.
Lawson ditches and is badly injured. Hoover makes a forced landing. Doolittle’s crew parachutes into the mountains. Chinese villagers, soldiers and others shelter the survivors and help them escape.
Hallmark ditches off the coast; Dieter and Fitzmaurice drown. Faktor dies after Gray’s bailout. Eight airmen from Hallmark’s and Farrow’s crews will fall into Japanese hands.
The remaining China-bound aircraft are abandoned or wrecked. Fifteen aircraft are lost in China; one is impounded in the USSR. Sixty-four airmen evade capture in China, aided by their rescuers.

Aftermath, 1942–45. Japan executes Hallmark, Farrow and Spatz in October 1942; Meder dies in captivity in 1943. Four prisoners survive to liberation. In China, the subsequent Japanese campaign brings massacres and biological warfare; the often-cited 250,000 deaths is an uncertain estimate.

On 21 April, Roosevelt says the bombers came from “our new secret base at Shangri-La!” The name conceals Hornet. The raid lifts American morale and strengthens support for Japan’s Midway operation; it did not originate that plan.
